newsitem.title: UK: Clinton's Bosnia troops plan upset allies -Britain.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's Bosnia troops plan upset allies -Britain.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has caused anxiety among Washington's allies by failing to consult them before announcing plans for deploying U.S. troops to Bosnia, a top British official said on Tuesday.

Clinton said after being re-elected earlier this month that he planned to send 8,500 troops to Bosnia for 18 months as part of an international force to replace the United Nation's Implementation Force (IFOR) which will withdraw in December.
He said a further 4-5,000 troops would be deployed to the region as possible reinforcements in an emergency.

But Emyr Jones Parry, deputy political director at the Foreign Office, told parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee that other countries who had agreed in principle to supply troops for the new force had expected their tour of duty to be 12 months.

"There was a certain amount of consternation because everyone had been assuming a force for one year and the Americans in that announcement, without any prior consultation, announced 18 months," Jones Parry said.
"There then followed an accelerated consideration in Brussels (where NATO has its headquarters) of what the Americans had proposed and how it should be taken forward."

Members of the committee asked Sir Nicholas Bonsor, the Foreign Office minister responsible for relations with the former Yugoslavia, whether Britain had protested to the U.S. administration about the lack of consultation.
"I am not aware that we have made any specific representations, but of course what the Americans have done is not binding on anyone else," he replied.
"It will be a matter of continuing negotiation as to whether the timing is indeed 12 months or 18 months. That is something which the allies will have to decide together."
Bonsor said Defence Secretary Michael Portillo will announce on Friday the number of troops Britain plans to contribute to the new international force.
He declined to confirm reports that it will send 5,000 men, but said it would almost certainly be the second largest national contingent after the Americans.
Britain hosts an international conference on the civilian aspects of peace implementation in Bosnia on Wednesday and Thursday of next week in London.

Jones Parry said Britain wanted the meeting to spell out to the parties in Bosnia that international aid to help it recover from its bloody civil war depended on implementation of the Dayton peace accord, particularly its arms control provisions.
"What we plan to do...is to ensure that the whole structure of the London conclusions will involve an immense amount of conditionality, a real biting conditionality on the parties," he said.
